title: A transcriptional biosensor reveals mechanisms of α-ketoglutarate signaling to chromatin.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and opened both GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) processed files for GSE325502: GSE325502_count.txt.gz is 56,184 gene rows x 36 mouse-brain samples of raw read counts (groups WT-Veh n=10, WT-aKG n=8, KO-Veh n=10, KO-aKG n=8; library sizes 5.8-13.3 million reads), and GSE325502_CPM_plasmidsaurus.csv.gz is the same experiment as counts-per-million for 21,637 genes. I computed that 36,686 genes have any non-zero count and 15,068 have >=10 counts in >=18 samples. I listed the GSE325503 file directory: only 6 merged bigWig coverage tracks (K4me3/K9me3/K27me3, one WT and one KO file each, 144-254 MB), no peak calls and no per-replicate tables. I read the full text on PubMed Central including the data-availability statement and the CRISPR screening methods.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The CRISPR knockout screen targeted 127 genes and yielded 4 gene-level hits (BCAT1, DLD, GPT2, SLC25A11); the screen tables (data S1, S2) and the genome-wide chromatin and expression tables (data S3-S8, 18 KB to 4 MB Excel files) could not be opened: Europe PMC reports the article as not open access, and the PubMed Central supplementary-file endpoints returned a challenge page instead of the files. Counts of '>800 genes downregulated and H3K27-hypermethylated' and '>1,200 genes H3K4me3-hypermethylated and overexpressed' come from the text only.

a1_downloadable.note: Both GEO series are public and I downloaded them without login; the paper's supplementary Excel tables (data S1-S8) were NOT retrievable (Europe PMC says not open access, PubMed Central /bin/ links blocked).

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. Nothing in the deposited files is a prediction target: GSE325502 is a raw count matrix and GSE325503 is raw coverage tracks. Any label (knockout-vs-wildtype expression change, or change in a histone mark at a gene) must first be built by running a differential analysis and, for chromatin, by binning 1.3 GB of bigWig signal into gene windows.

a3_inputs_present.note: Not the blocker: inputs would be mouse genomic sequence pulled from a reference genome by gene symbol, which is a standard lookup, not thousands of manual resolutions.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are clear in the files I opened: integer read counts in count.txt.gz and counts-per-million in the CPM file; bigWig tracks are coverage, normalisation method not stated in the directory listing.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL. The independent unit is the animal: 36 RNA-seq brain samples in four groups, 21 ChIP-seq libraries collapsed into 6 merged tracks (3 mice per genotype per mark), and a 127-gene CRISPR screen. Gene rows (56,184) are not independent examples — they all come from one perturbation contrast in one tissue of one mouse line.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Verified sizes: count matrix 1.3 MB gzipped, CPM 3.0 MB gzipped; the six bigWig files total about 1.3 GB, each above the 50 MB single-file cap but streamable. Size is not the problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The file's 36 columns match the paper's stated design exactly (n = 10 vehicle and n = 8 dm-αKG per genotype), and GEO lists 36 RNA-seq and 21 ChIP-seq samples as described.

a8_label_provenance.note: No label exists to trace, so no circularity: counts and coverage are direct sequencing measurements, not another model's output.

existing_models.name: AlphaGenome (DeepMind sequence-to-function DNA model, Nature 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported by its authors to match or beat the best external models in 25 of 26 variant-effect evaluations; I did not retrieve the per-task numbers or splits in this evaluation.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved — I only read search summaries, not the paper.

existing_models.name: Enformer (sequence-to-expression and histone-mark model)
existing_models.score_and_split: Predicts thousands of human and mouse genomic tracks from 200 kb of sequence; specific numbers not retrieved here.

backbone.name: AlphaGenome or Enformer (DNA sequence models that already output histone-mark and expression tracks for mouse)
backbone.hardware: CPU feasible only for a few thousand gene windows; a GPU would be wanted for genome-wide inference.
backbone.licence: AlphaGenome weights are non-commercial; Enformer is openly available. Not pursued because the data fails Part A.

integration.partner_dataset: Mouse ENCODE / public H3K27me3 and H3K4me3 brain tracks, and IDH-mutant glioma datasets where α-ketoglutarate signalling is also disturbed
integration.join_key: Mouse gene symbol or Ensembl gene ID, plus mm39/mm10 genomic coordinates
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do the genes that gain repressive methylation when the α-ketoglutarate supply is cut in mouse brain overlap the genes silenced in human tumours with the same metabolic lesion — a question this one experiment alone cannot answer, and which needs only a gene list, not a model.

controls.positive_control: Gpt2 itself must be the most depleted gene in the knockout count matrix — a one-line check that confirms the sample labels are right.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle genotype labels across the 36 samples and confirm the differential-expression signal collapses.
controls.external_validation: None usable within this paper: there is a single genotype contrast in a single tissue, so any held-out set is drawn from the same experiment.

honest_claim_h3: Any model built on these files could only claim to describe which genes changed in one bulk RNA-sequencing contrast between Gpt2-knockout and wild-type mouse brain (and one merged chromatin track per mark), with no independent perturbation, tissue or cohort to test whether the pattern generalises.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use DNA sequence around each gene to predict which genes lose expression and gain repressive chromatin marks when a metabolic enzyme is knocked out.
plain_idea.train_on: Gene windows from the mouse genome paired with the change seen between Gpt2-knockout and wild-type brain. Verified counts: 56,184 gene rows but only 36 animals and one knockout-versus-wild-type contrast, plus 6 merged chromatin tracks.
plain_idea.predict: A per-gene change score — either the expression log fold-change computed from the deposited read counts, or the change in H3K27me3/H3K4me3 signal that would have to be quantified from the bigWig coverage tracks.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Researchers studying GPT2 deficiency and α-ketoglutarate-linked tumours would like to know which genes are vulnerable when this metabolite runs short; but with one contrast and no second cohort, a model here would be fitting a single experiment rather than learning a rule.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: predict, from mouse genomic sequence or promoter CpG content, which genes are downregulated and H3K27me3-hypermethylated when nuclear α-ketoglutarate is depleted by Gpt2 loss, using a frozen DNA sequence model with a new head. The deposited data supports a classical differential-expression analysis, not a supervised learning problem: one perturbation contrast, 36 animals, merged chromatin tracks with no replicate-level processed files, and a 127-gene CRISPR screen.

effort.compute_note: Measured file sizes directly (1.3 MB + 3.0 MB gzipped tables, six bigWigs of 144-254 MB). The 20 hours is an estimate for running a differential-expression analysis plus binning the bigWig tracks into gene windows; nothing was timed because the project was rejected at Part A.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the independent biological units before anything else: 36 RNA-seq animals and one genotype contrast. That number, which took one command on the downloaded count matrix, kills the project.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A2 and A5 in the files I opened. The deposited data is a 36-sample bulk RNA-sequencing count matrix plus six merged chromatin coverage tracks — there is no label column anywhere, any target would have to be constructed by running a differential analysis, and the independent sample size (36 animals, one knockout contrast, a 127-gene CRISPR screen) is one to two orders of magnitude below what supervised learning needs. The paper is an excellent piece of biology and a genuinely new biosensor tool, but its data is designed for hypothesis testing, not model training.
